claims.statement: Sebastian's only inbound integration is `app.MapGitHubWebhooks(secret: config.GitHub.WebhookSecret)` next to a `/health` endpoint; the host registers no authentication middleware, so the HMAC webhook secret (required, non-blank, read once from the `IOptions<SebastianConfig>` snapshot at composition time) is the sole trust boundary and rotating it requires a process restart.

`WebhookEventProcessor` is registered through an explicit constructor-call factory rather than `AddSingleton<WebhookEventProcessor, GitHubWebhookProcessor>()` because `GitHubWebhookProcessor` is `internal sealed`; the factory also fixes the processor's four dependencies (`ILogger<GitHubWebhookProcessor>`, `GitHubService`, `JobQueue`, `Git`) at the registration site, so the processor is constructed on the first delivery rather than at boot.

Sebastian overrides only the `IssuesEvent` and `PushEvent` handlers; every other GitHub event type reaches the base `WebhookEventProcessor` dispatch and produces no routing, queue call, or GitHub write, and neither event override calls `base`, so Sebastian's behavior is the whole behavior for those two events. `ProcessWebhookAsync` is overridden only to log each delivery before delegating to base dispatch.

The issues path gates twice before any work: the action must be one of `Opened`, `Labeled`, `Edited`, `Reopened`, and the issue must be `IssueState.Open` and carry a label named `feature` compared with `OrdinalIgnoreCase`; every other delivery returns with no log, no comment, and no state change, which is why `bug`-labeled issues are dropped and a closed issue can never be re-validated or re-queued by an edit.

After the action and state/label gates, a third guard returns silently when `Repository`, `Repository.Owner.Login`, or `Repository.Name` is null, while `Repository.FullName` falls back to the literal `"unknown"` for logging only — so a malformed payload is invisible in logs and never throws.

Spec validation is ordered before the `ready-for-agent` gate: when `SpecTemplateValidator.FindMissingSections` reports gaps the processor posts a comment naming the sections and then closes the issue as `not_planned` (two sequential GitHub writes inside the request) before returning, so a maintainer's approval never overrides the input contract, and validation re-runs on every later qualifying delivery.

A valid `feature` spec that also carries `ready-for-agent` is turned into `ImplementSpec(owner, name, issueNumber, title, body)` — a snapshot of the delivery payload — and handed to `JobQueue.TryAdd`, whose boolean is treated as informational: `true` logs `Started implementation` at Information, `false` logs `already running` at Debug, and neither path throws, comments, or retries; a valid spec without the label produces no action and no log at all.

Push handling bypasses the job queue entirely: `ProcessPushWebhookAsync` logs every push (including branch pushes and deletions) and then awaits `git.SyncMainAsync(pushEvent.Ref, pushEvent.Deleted, cancellationToken)` inline in the request, with a `// shortcut:` comment acknowledging the latency tradeoff; the ref filter that makes non-`main` and deleted refs no-ops lives in `Git.SyncMainAsync` (`StringComparison.Ordinal` on `refs/heads/main`), not in the processor.

The two handlers have opposite failure policies: `ProcessIssuesWebhookAsync` has no `try`/`catch`, so a failing comment or close escapes into the Octokit middleware and becomes a failed delivery GitHub may redeliver (re-posing the comment), while `PushWebhookAsync` inherits `Git.SyncMainAsync`'s swallow behavior that logs `InvalidOperationException` at Warning and `OperationCanceledException` at Debug and always acknowledges the delivery. The webhook push sync also has no timeout of its own, unlike the ten-second bounded startup sync.

Intake does not verify that the issue's repository matches the local clone: any repository's qualifying `feature` issue is enqueued, and the mismatch is detected later by `ImplementSpec.PrepareWorkspaceAsync`, which throws and lets `JobQueue` log `Job {Key} failed` at Error.

Logging is the only observability of routing decisions: `LogReceived` emits an Information line with the event type and header event for every delivery before dispatch, so a delivery that logs only that line was filtered, and the two explanatory branches (invalid spec, duplicate suppression) are the only ones emitted at Debug/Information — the silent returns and the valid-but-not-ready branch emit nothing.

No test exercises `GitHubWebhookProcessor` or the endpoint — there is no webhook routing test and no `WebApplicationFactory` in the suite — so the routing policy is unpinned; what is pinned at the unit level is the delegated logic (the section contract via `SpecTemplateValidatorTests` and admission semantics via `JobQueueTests`), reachable because `Sebastian.csproj` grants `InternalsVisibleTo` to `Sebastian.Tests`.

Sebastian's only inbound integration is app.MapGitHubWebhooks(secret: config.GitHub.WebhookSecret) alongside a /health route; the secret is read once at composition time from GitHub:WebhookSecret (a [Required] string), so the HMAC trust boundary cannot be rotated without a process restart, and no authentication middleware exists anywhere in the host.

GitHubWebhookProcessor is registered under the abstract WebhookEventProcessor via a factory lambda (not AddSingleton<TService, TImpl>) because the concrete type is internal and must stay out of reflection-based construction; its four dependencies — ILogger<GitHubWebhookProcessor>, GitHubService, JobQueue, and Git — are all root singletons, and this registration is a lazy singleton constructed on the first delivery, so a construction failure is a failed webhook request rather than a failed deployment (unlike GitHubService and ProviderResolver, which Program.cs resolves eagerly).

The ProcessWebhookAsync override emits exactly one Information line, 'Webhook {EventType} ({Event})', for every signature-verified delivery before base dispatch, and that line carries no action, repository, issue number, or X-GitHub-Delivery id — so logs prove a delivery arrived and its model/header type but not what it concerned, and a redelivery is indistinguishable from a fresh event.

ProcessIssuesWebhookAsync short-circuits silently (no log, no comment, no state change) unless the action is exactly Opened, Labeled, Edited, or Reopened; additional silent guards require the payload issue's State to be Open with a 'feature' label (OrdinalIgnoreCase) and require Repository, Owner.Login, and Name to be non-null before the two GitHub writes can be called.

In the issue path, SpecTemplateValidator.FindMissingSections runs and returns before the ready-for-agent check, so an issue already approved with ready-for-agent is still commented on and closed as not_planned when a required section is empty, and an invalid spec is never enqueued (the close path ends in a return).

A complete spec issue carrying 'feature' and 'ready-for-agent' becomes an ImplementSpec job built from the webhook payload's title and body (never re-fetched), and the boolean from JobQueue.TryAdd is informational only: true logs Information 'Started implementation for {Repository}#{Number}', false logs Debug 'Implementation already running for {Repository}#{Number}' with no throw and no comment.

Both gate labels are read-only const filters ('feature' and 'ready-for-agent', matched OrdinalIgnoreCase via HasLabel); the processor never writes a label and never verifies which actor applied one, so the entire state transition into agent work is enforced by humans.

Only ProcessIssuesWebhookAsync and ProcessPushWebhookAsync are overridden; every other GitHub event type (pull_request, issue_comment, ping, workflow_run, and the unhandled issue actions) reaches the base processor's dispatch after the delivery log line and produces no side effect, which is why no command surface such as a merge command exists.

The three issue guards log nothing by design — the delivery line already records arrival, rejected traffic dominates at installation scope, and a skip is not an error — with the consequence that at the default Information level the only visible intake outcomes are 'a delivery arrived' and 'implementation started'; the invalid-spec closure and the duplicate-key rejection are Debug only.

The invalid-spec path performs two sequential, non-idempotent GitHub writes (PostCommentAsync then CloseIssueAsync with state_reason not_planned) with no try/catch and no delivery-id dedupe, so a redelivered 'open with missing sections' payload passes the payload-state guard again and posts a second comment and a second close attempt; a failure on the comment leaves the issue untouched while a failure on the close leaves a comment on an open issue.

ProcessPushWebhookAsync logs Information 'Push {RefName} on {Repository}: {Before} -> {After}' and then awaits git.SyncMainAsync(pushEvent.Ref, pushEvent.Deleted, cancellationToken) inline inside the request, under a documented 'shortcut: synchronous fetch in the webhook; move to a background queue if delivery latency becomes a problem' comment — making push handling the only git work on a request thread and the webhook response time a real constraint for anything added to intake.

The push-triggered SyncMainAsync is a ref filter first: it returns before invoking any git command when the push was a deletion or the ref is not exactly refs/heads/main (Ordinal), so pushes to sebastian/issue-<n> and other branches produce an Information log line with no mirror update.

A push-triggered sync cannot fail the webhook request because SyncMainAsync catches InvalidOperationException (logged Warning, 'Local main sync failed') and OperationCanceledException (logged Debug, 'Local main sync cancelled'); the processor itself has no try/catch, so any other exception type thrown from the sync or from a GitHub write propagates out of the handler as a failed request, and JobQueue is the only error-isolating boundary in the process (downstream of intake).

The webhook call site of SyncMainAsync is unbounded: unlike Git.StartAsync, which runs the same sync under a linked CancellationTokenSource with CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)), the push handler passes only the request cancellation token, so a slow git fetch --prune origin adds its full duration to the delivery response and a client disconnect cancels the fetch with a Debug-only log.

The payload repository is never cross-checked at intake: the processor comments on and closes whichever issue a delivery names, and the owner/repository match against the parsed origin remote is enforced only later, in ImplementSpec.PrepareWorkspaceAsync, for the implementation path.

No test exercises GitHubWebhookProcessor: the suite has no WebApplicationFactory, no integration test of Program.cs, and no reference to the processor, so the action list, label comparisons, silent returns, validation-before-approval ordering, and inline push sync rest on review alone; the nearest coverage pins its dependencies — SpecTemplateValidatorTests for the section contract and JobQueueTests for duplicate-key rejection — and adding a processor test requires first introducing a seam, because the class takes concrete GitHubService, Git, and JobQueue singletons.
